report.summary: Payment write failures on payment-service (error rate about 28-32% from 12:00 UTC) and the downstream checkout-service retries (about 12-13%) are attributed by the system's conclusive determination to exhaustion of the payments-db data volume, with ENOSPC 'could not extend file' errors from 11:59:29Z and disk_used_pct near or above 100% from 11:50Z. Connections, CPU, latency and replication lag stayed flat, which argues against load or connection-pool causes. The leading hypothesis has confidence 0.75 with a margin of 0.55 over the runner-up, and 27% of evidence is contradicting. The v3.1.4 deploy at 09:55Z (logging-only, described as 'more detailed request logging') remains an unresolved alternative because the diff was not retrieved and it is unknown whether its logs are written to the database volume. The SQLSTATE 53100 code is masked in tool output and was not found in database logs, so the storage cause rests on the ENOSPC message text and disk metric rather than the SQLSTATE. Disk values above 100% are unexplained and may be a metric artifact.

root_cause.mechanism: The payments-db data volume ran out of space: disk_used_pct stepped from 87.8% at 11:00Z to about 98.5% at 11:40Z and above 100% by 11:50Z, and ENOSPC errors on base/16384/24576 begin at 11:59:29Z. Payment INSERTs then fail with 'could not extend file' from 12:00:21Z, which payment-service surfaces as a roughly 28-32% error rate, and checkout sees failed payment calls and retries.

inferred_conclusions.statement: The payment write failures are most likely caused by exhaustion of the payments-db data volume, which caused INSERT failures from 11:59Z and surfaced as the payment-service error-rate jump at 12:00Z.

brief.alert: ALERT [P1] payment-service error rate 30% since ~12:00 UTC. payment-service was deployed earlier today.

plan.incident_understanding: payment-service error rate jumped to about 30% since roughly 12:00 UTC, following a deployment earlier today; checkout-service is also alerting, suggesting propagation of payment write failures. Telemetry covers 11:00-12:30 UTC.

Downstream datastore or dependency of payment-service degraded or rejecting writes, independent of the deployment
Configuration or feature flag change coupled with the deployment triggered the failures
Checkout-service change or retry storm amplifying errors rather than originating them

findings.summary: Payment-service failed payment writes are dominated by one signature: "INSERT INTO payments failed: could not extend file: No space left on device (SQLSTATE 53100)". The payment-service error rate jumped from about 0.2% to about 28% in the 12:00 UTC bucket. Checkout-service error rate jumped in the same 12:00 bucket, from about 0.3% to about 12-13%. Checkout's own logs contain no ERROR lines in the window, only retry warnings. The earliest logged checkout retry (12:00:08) precedes the first logged payment ERROR (12:00:21) by about 13 seconds, but both sit in the same 5-minute metric bucket, so the metrics alone do not establish which service moved first.

observations.statement: payment-service has 37 WARN/ERROR lines from 11:00 to 12:30 UTC: 35 ERROR, all the same signature 'INSERT INTO payments failed: could not extend file: No space left on device (SQLSTATE 53100)', and 2 WARN 'payment-provider responded in #ms' lines (at 11:21:54 and 12:12:49).
The first payment-service ERROR is at 12:00:21Z (SQLSTATE 53100, disk full on the payments insert path). No payment-service ERROR lines appear between 11:00 and 12:00:21.
payment-service error_rate was flat at 0.15-0.25% from 11:00 to 11:55, then 28.19% in the 12:00 bucket. It stayed between 27.9% and 32.0% through 12:30 (max 32.03% at 12:25).
checkout-service error_rate was 0.25-0.34% from 11:00 to 11:55, then 12.47% in the 12:00 bucket. It stayed between 12.2% and 13.6% through 12:30 (max 13.57% at 12:05).

checkout-service has no ERROR-level lines in the window. Its 4 WARN lines are: a slow inventory reservation at 11:01:02 (1148ms), a retry of the idempotent call to payment-service (attempt 2) at 11:22:30, a retry at 12:00:08, and a slow inventory reservation at 12:21:50 (1293ms).
The checkout-service retry warnings begin at 12:00:08, after the 11:22:30 baseline retry. That is about 13 seconds before the first payment-service ERROR at 12:00:21.
Payment-provider latency warnings are sparse (2 in the window, at 11:21:54 and 12:12:49). They do not track the 12:00 onset, so provider latency does not look like the driver of the step change.
Payment-service ERROR lines recur roughly every 30-90 seconds from 12:00:21 to 12:30:00. This is a sustained failure rather than a single burst.

interpretations.statement: The payment write failures are caused by the database or storage layer running out of disk space (SQLSTATE 53100, 'could not extend file'), not by application code. The error text points at the database file system.

Checkout-service errors are a downstream effect of the payment-service failures. The checkout retry warnings start at the same time as the payment failures, and checkout reports no independent error signature.

Payment-service errors start at 12:00 UTC and checkout errors also start at 12:00 UTC, so onset is simultaneous at 5-minute resolution. The 13-second retry lead in checkout is too small to settle ordering. The timing argues against checkout being an independent origin, but it does not prove the order.

data_gaps: checkout-service has no ERROR-level logs in the window, so its own failure signature cannot be seen; only WARN retries are visible.
The SQLSTATE code is masked as '#' in the tool output, so the exact code is inferred from the text only.
Metrics are at 5-minute resolution, so sub-bucket ordering between payment and checkout onset cannot be resolved.

The growth source is unidentified, so H2 cannot be dismissed. Because no further tool calls are available, the conclusion should be stated as payments-db storage exhaustion with the v3.1.4 logging-to-volume question explicitly unresolved and confidence capped accordingly.

issues.detail: Confidence 0.75 is reasonable, but the 'disk_used_pct above 100%' values are unexplained and the SQLSTATE is inferred from message text. The report should state that the storage cause is established by the ENOSPC log text and disk metric, not by the SQLSTATE.

H2 is a competing cause that fits the evidence as well on the disk side: if v3.1.4 request/payload logging writes to the payments-db volume, that would explain both disk growth and the ENOSPC errors. The analysis cannot rule this out because the growth source and the v3.1.4 diff were never retrieved. The root cause on the storage side therefore may be a deployment regression rather than an independent storage event.

H2 lists L0189 as contradicting, but L0189 is a payments-db ENOSPC error that does not by itself contradict a logging-driven disk fill; it only shows that the disk was full. The contradiction is weaker than stated.

The claim that the storage event started at 11:59:29 is overstated: disk was at 98.5% from 11:40Z and above 100% by 11:50Z, so the first ERROR marks when writes failed, not when storage was exhausted. The analysis partially acknowledges this but the mechanism text still frames 11:59 as the onset.
H3 is low confidence and well contradicted by flat connections (M37) and explicit ENOSPC messages. Its listed support (P07) is a past incident and cannot count as proof for this one.

Free-space bytes, growth source and the 10:00–11:00Z baseline are missing, but the tools are exhausted, so this cannot be obtained now and should be reported as an unresolved gap rather than a reason to defer the conclusion.

reasons: confidence 0.75, margin 0.55, 8 verified supporting and 3 contradicting evidence items (27%)
